# Summary of Information on Philip Rubin
Philip Rubin is an accomplished scientist whose interdisciplinary research integrates computational, engineering, linguistic, physiological, and psychological methods to study embodied cognition, particularly the biological bases of speech and language. Notably, Rubin developed foundational computational models and software systems in speech synthesis and perception, such as ASY (articulatory synthesis program), SWS (sinewave synthesis program), CASY (configurable articulatory synthesizer), and TADA (a task-dynamic modeling system). His work on articulatory and sinewave synthesis has been pioneering since the 1970s, contributing significant theoretical advances on gestures, events, and perceptual organization in speech. Rubin has also been actively involved in exploring audiovisual speech and multimodal integration.
Beyond research, Rubin has played significant roles in science policy and advocacy, including chairing the National Academies Board on Behavioral, Cognitive, and Sensory Sciences, serving at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) as Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences, and leading various committees related to human subjects research ethics and scientific oversight. He has contributed to modernizing human subjects protections and has critiqued ineffective technologies in national security contexts. Rubin has been recognized with numerous fellowships and honors, serves on multiple scientific boards and advisory committees, and has been involved in education innovation and science advocacy. Additionally, his work in sine-wave speech synthesis has inspired cultural references, such as the similarity to sounds like R2-D2 in media.
